CHAIR ( Senator Ciccone ): I declare open this meeting of the Senate Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee. I want to begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and paying my respects to their elders past and present. The Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of the proposed expenditure for the year 2025-26 and other related documents for the Foreign Affairs and Trade, and Defence portfolios. The committee may also examine the annual reports of the departments and agencies appearing before it. The committee is due to report to the Senate on 31 March this year. The committee has set 13 March as the deadline for senators to submit written questions on notice for the purpose of this hearing. The committee has also set 24 April as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice for the purpose of this hearing.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as contempt. It's also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence.

The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy and does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policy or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. I draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009 specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised and which I now incorporate into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

CHAIR: Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement claiming that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets the requirements of the 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to articulate the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or the document.

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. I ask members of the media to follow the established media guidelines and instructions of the committee secretariat. Witnesses and senators who are seeking to table documents during the committee's hearings are requested to provide an electronic copy, if you can do so, to the secretariat so we can circulate them during the hearing.

Department of Veterans' Affairs

[18:36]

CHAIR: I'd like to commence today's hearing and acknowledge representatives from the Department of Veterans' Affairs. I welcome Senator the Hon. Jenny McAllister, who is representing the Minister for Veterans' Affairs; Ms Alison Frame, the secretary of the Department of Veterans' Affairs; and officers of the department. Good evening, Minister. Do you have an opening statement?

Senator McAllister: No.

CHAIR: Ms Frame, do you have an opening statement?

Ms Frame : I do.

CHAIR: Are you happy to table that at the conclusion?

Ms Frame : Yes, I am.

CHAIR: Thank you. You have the call.

Ms Frame : Thank you. 2026 will be a significant year for the Department of Veterans' Affairs as we continue to implement key recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. Two critical recommendations accepted by government will become a reality from 1 July.

Firstly, the Veterans' Entitlements, Treatment and Support (Simplification and Harmonisation) Act 2025 will come into force and see veterans and families of veterans able to receive the supports they need and deserve faster, leading to improved outcomes. New claims for compensation and rehabilitation received on or after 1 July will be determined under an improved version of the Military Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 2004 as the single ongoing act. This will provide a single clearer pathway for accessing support and make it easier for veterans to understand and navigate. DVA continues to communicate extensively with the veteran community and advocate about the upcoming changes so that they are well informed and can plan for their individual circumstances.

Secondly, the new veteran and family wellbeing agency will begin operation. The recent Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook provided $78 million over four years to establish the agency, which implements recommendation 87 of the royal commission's final report and provides the coordinated delivery of related recommendations 80, 81 and 86. The agency will focus on the successful transition from military to civilian life, community connection and improving wellbeing. Initially, the agency will focus on supporting at-risk veterans transitioning from the ADF with a view to expanding capability as the agency grows.

These two milestones are the culmination of extensive consultative and developmental work by DVA staff, and I thank them for their extraordinary efforts as we bring these initiatives to fruition. The work also builds on the significant progress achieved in 2025 on delivering the government's response to the royal commission, with 32 recommendations implemented by the end of last year.

The establishment of the wellbeing agency and other initiatives underscores a shift to a deeper focus across DVA and the entire veteran support system on the wellbeing of veterans and families of veterans. In MYEFO, the government provided $739.2 million over four years to facilitate better long-term health and wellbeing outcomes for veterans, including prioritising upfront early intervention and treatment, incentivising the provision of mental health care plans and a national PTSD treatment study. This improved access to treatment will support veterans to receive the right care as early as possible, supporting their long-term wellbeing and improving their quality of life.

Claims for compensation continue to increase year on year. Claims received in the financial year to January 2026 constitute a 10 per cent increase on the record numbers received last year. In response to this, however, DVA teams continue to make record determinations, and, most importantly, the vast majority of initial liability claims are being allocated within 14 days. MRCA initial liability claims received and determined in the last 12 months took on average around 120 days to process, which means that veterans are getting access to the health services and payments they may need while follow-on claims for permanent impairment are being assessed.

From next week, DVA will commence a pilot with the Queensland RSL using AI to support the preparation of summaries to assist delegates in making initial liability claims. The pilot operates on a voluntary consent basis and is subject to strict privacy and information security standards. To improve processing times for permanent impairment claims, we are in the process of bringing in additional resources to review claims and confirm if the medical reports and information on record are adequate to enable a delegate decision and to implement an outbound call strategy to update veterans on the progress of their claims.

In addition to these efforts to improve processing efficiency, DVA's work to strengthen the integrity of the veteran support system continues at pace. In MYEFO, the government provided $203.1 million over four years to strengthen DVA's provider integrity capability, support free veteran advocacy services, combat fraud activity and support the operations of the new Institute of Veterans' Advocacy. The department stood up a new provider integrity division last December. The team is focused on detecting and addressing unethical and fraudulent practices by service providers and advocates. I put on the record that the vast majority do the right thing; however, there are those who do not, and we are committed to ensuring veterans are not exploited and their own entitlements are not eroded by unnecessary fees.

In December 2025, the government tabled its response to the Senate inquiry into issues relating to advocacy services for veterans accessing compensation and income support, agreeing or agreeing in principle to six of the committee's seven recommendations. Consistent with the committee's recommendation that DVA explore potential legislative action to curb harmful and deceptive business practices in the commercial advocacy sector, which was agreed by government, public consultation is now underway on options to better protect veterans. We are also working closely with the Institute of Veterans' Advocacy, which has been established as the national professional association for veterans advocates and to set competency and training standards for the sector. I am pleased to note the IVA recently announced it is accepting membership applications. I thank the committee, and I look forward to your questions.

CHAIR: Thanks, Ms Frame. Senator Scarr.

Senator SCARR: I've been in contact with medical providers in my home state of Queensland and also with the AMA Queensland branch, and they've raised a number of disturbing issues with me. The first issue I want to raise with you is: the department appears to have sent out letters to practice managers in relation to raising issues with respect to billing practices, but in those letters—I've got one here—it says, 'If irregular or suspected fraudulent behaviour is identified, DVA will institute measures to ensure ongoing compliance, including the referral of matters to regulatory bodies and/or Australian Federal Police for investigation.' Can you understand, for a medical practice that is dealing with your department and seeking clarification with respect to numerous matters and not getting that clarification, how aggrieved they feel when they get a letter potentially referring them to the Australian Federal Police? Do you think that's the right approach to deal with medical practitioners who, in many cases, are making personal sacrifices to provide medical care to our veterans?

Ms Frame : I'll commence, and then I'll hand to my colleague here, Mr Kefford, who can provide more detail. I would say that in those letters we are providing relevant information to medical professionals. We are not saying we are referring people. We are providing advice about what is available to the department, and that is obviously referring to an escalation at the end of the letter there. I would also advise the committee tonight that we have, in fact, referred some medical professionals to Ahpra and to the AFP, so we are merely advising medical professionals that this has occurred. We're not saying to the people who receive those letters, 'This is happening to you'; we are providing information that this is happening where we are not satisfied that processes are being followed.

Senator SCARR: We'll get to the further answer, but this is a letter to professionals who are providing a service. I put it to you that in the first instance—where you're seeking clarification in a one-page letter—there shouldn't be any mention of referrals to the Australian Federal Police. You should simply try to seek clarification in relation to matters rather than mention referrals to the police. The impact of that letter is demonstrated by the fact that it's been raised with me by medical practitioners how aggrieved they are. Will you take it on board? Will you take on notice the fact that maybe there's a better approach to this than initial letters referring to references to the Australian Federal Police?

Ms Frame : I will. I would also just like to take on notice whether that letter is in fact the first letter. It may well be; I know we've sent previous letters. I don't know if my colleagues at the table know anything more. So that is something that we will have a look at regarding that letter. And it may be that we can clarify that the one you're holding up is not, in fact, the first letter that's gone out.

Mr Kefford : As the secretary referred to, there are a range of measures we can take when we do have concerns about the behaviour of medical providers. As was acknowledged in the opening statement, we do recognise that the majority of providers who work with us are doing the right thing. However, as you know from evidence in other sittings of this committee, we have had concerns in recent times about the behaviour of medical providers, whether that relates to the amounts being charged or indeed the quantum of tests being ordered. And we've taken regulatory action in relation to that. I think I know, because of the way you introduced it, who you are particularly talking about. I won't name them; you haven't. But what I can say is that there have been significant discussions since that letter, including as recently as in the last few weeks. I won't go any further or identify—forgive me.

There's guidance in our treatment notes and in our documents for doctors engaging with our system. It's important—and it is an area where DVA has needed to be more active in recent times—that, as part of that education process, we say that there are a range of options we can take, up to and including the referrals that have been made. Clearly, that's not our first and only response. But I think that in terms of signalling the depths of concern that we have, it is important to note—as with all Commonwealth agencies—the range of options that are open to us.

Senator SCARR: Yes. I don't think that's the most constructive approach. My next question is: does DVA pay the same fee to all providers for compensation medical assessments?

Mr Kefford : We have in the last few weeks published updated guidance on reasonable fees. But the fees in that context are not determined in the way that our treatment fees are.

Senator SCARR: Let me repeat the question: does DVA pay the same fee to all providers for compensation medical assessments?

Mr Kefford : No, it's not a prescribed fee.

Senator SCARR: Why?

Mr Kefford : The statutory basis is that the department is required to pay reasonable fees. So there has been guidance, as I said, that's been updated. But, at the end of the day, that part of the system doesn't have prescribed fees in the way that the treatment part of the system does.

Senator SCARR: So why is the department paying different fees for compensation medical assessments undertaken by different providers?

Mr Kefford : In a sense, we're paying the bills that are presented along with the claims. It's our obligation under the act to pay those.

Senator SCARR: Sorry, Mr Kefford, why are you using differential fees? Why are you paying fees on a differential basis? Why are you paying different providers different fees for providing compensation medical assessment?

Mr Kefford : Well, as I've described, they're not prescribed fees. And so—

Senator SCARR: I didn't say they were. I said you're paying different fees for compensation medical assessments undertaken by different providers. Correct?

Mr Kefford : That's correct.

Senator SCARR: Why?

Mr Kefford : That's been a feature of our system for some time. I've explained the basis on which we do it.

Senator SCARR: I'm sorry, but you haven't explained the basis on which you do it. And, with respect, saying that it's been a feature of the system for some time is probably the worst possible explanation I could receive. The question I have, and this has been raised by the Australian Medical Association of Queensland, is about why the department is providing different providers with different fees for compensation medical assessments. I'm asking why.

Ms Frame : If I could just add, Mr Kefford has referred to the very recent guidance we put out to try and address that issue and provide some range, from the department, or a guidance on fees about what the department considers to be a fair price for compensation assessment. But where assessors, medical professionals, are able to demonstrate and provide to the department evidence of a more complex assessment or whatever additional measures they have undertaken in completing an assessment, the department looks at that information and has the ability to pay above that guidance, if that is demonstrated to be a legitimate claim.

Mr Brown : I'd have to look at the specific examples that have been raised with you, but we do pay a differential based on a short consultation, long consultation and per page for a report. Some of the differences in the amounts we're paying to providers might be due to the structure of the guidance that we put out as well.

Senator SCARR: I've been told—and this is by people who are actually providing these services—that particularly large providers are being paid more for doing this work than smaller providers, under contracts that have been entered into with the large providers. Is that the case?

Ms Frame : There are no contracts for compensation assessment, apart from mlcoa, which is the one that the department has, but veterans can go to whichever doctor they want to. We don't have multiple contracts for compensation assessment providers. We have one contract with mlcoa for independent medical examinations, and my colleagues here can tell you about the circumstances in which they are used, but the vast majority of compensation assessments are undertaken by any medical professionals who complete those assessments and they are not under contract to the department.

Senator SCARR: Ms Frame, you're not aware of the concern amongst providers of these important services that their clients—in many cases, clients they've established relationships with over a long period of time—are actually pressured to go to mlcoa? Are you aware of that concern?

Ms Frame : We can provide more information on—

Senator SCARR: Sorry, Ms Frame. Are you aware of that concern?

Ms Frame : I am, yes.

Senator SCARR: So why do people have that concern?

Ms Frame : I wouldn't express it in the terms you have: 'They are pressured to go to mlcoa.' We can talk about the parameters under which the department requests a veteran undertake an assessment with mlcoa.

Senator SCARR: Okay, please.

Mr Kefford : There are two circumstances. One is where a veteran is unable to find a doctor. We're able to refer them to mlcoa in that context.

Senator SCARR: I'm talking about circumstances where they've had a long-term relationship with the doctor and—

Mr Kefford : I was coming to the second part of my answer.

Senator SCARR: Sorry. For the record, they've had a long-term relationship with the medical practitioner, and medical practitioners are telling me their clients are being pressured to go to mlcoa.

Mr Kefford : There have been circumstances, particularly recently, where we have had concerns about the—and I'm not suggesting this in particular circumstances but in general terms—veracity of the reports in front of us or, indeed, where we are seeing complex claims lodged with multiple conditions, where we have referred veterans for independent medical examination. I wouldn't describe that as being pressured to go to mlcoa. It's where the department consciously decides to refer for an independent medical examination.

It is our preference that compensation reports are provided by treating doctors, but it's also been the practice of certain providers to deliberately split veterans away from their treating doctors, to go down a different path, usually involving commissions based advocacy services.

Senator SCARR: It appears that different rates are paid in certain circumstances. What's the current range of fees the department pays in relation to compensation medical assessments—feel free to take this on notice—and what factors determine the different payment rates?

Mr Kefford : We might table the schedule to which I referred in my earlier evidence because that has it, including the distinctions that Mr Brown drew, in terms of the time of the consultation and so on. We could table that this evening.

Senator SCARR: Just to be clear, as I'm understanding your evidence, DVA does not hold contracts with medical providers at different rates for compensation medical assessments.

Mr Kefford : To give you a clear answer, we have two sets of contractual arrangements with doctors. One is with mlcoa, for independent medical examinations, as I've described them. The other one is with Bupa, and that is for our internal medical advice to delegates. We do not have contracts with other treating doctors.

Senator SCARR: Okay, so what's—

CHAIR: We just need to finish up on this as I have to rotate the call, given the limited time we have tonight.

Senator SCARR: Okay—I'll let you rotate the call and I'll come back.

CHAIR: Thanks. Senator Shoebridge and then Senator Pocock.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Thanks, and I'll continue this line of questioning. I have to tell you that I've heard from the AMA in Queensland and also from doctors around the country that they feel like they're being treated as potential criminals, including through correspondence they're getting, simply by treating veterans and then writing reports and providing them to the department. They feel like they're being targeted in doing their job and writing reports about veterans. It isn't limited to one or two doctors; there's a sense out there that DVA is targeting them. I've seen similar correspondence, threatening to send them to the AFP. Are you unaware of this sense of concern amongst treating doctors?

Ms Frame : May I just provide some context to your question? I certainly want to emphasise, in response to Senator Scarr's questions as well, that we do meet regularly with medical professionals. The AMA—I understand that the Queensland AMA is now distinct from the federal AMA? Is that right?

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And I have met with them.

Ms Frame : We have met with both the Queensland AMA and the AMA. We have a General Practice Advisory Group in the department and we have regular interactions with medical professionals. But you heard me say in my opening statement that the government committed over $200 million to an integrity division in DVA in MYEFO last year. That's not a decision that's made in the absence of evidence of increasing core practice. I also said in my opening statement that most people do the right thing: medical professionals who we work very responsibly and collaboratively with—and have for many, many years—continue to do the right thing. However, there was observed behaviour; we saw it in billing practices and we saw it in veterans being referred to medical tests—many, many medical tests—that the Department of Veterans' Affairs did not wish them to undertake and did not require them to undertake. That's a circumstance where—this is to Senator Scarr as well—we would refer the veteran to mlcoa. I have heard stories and reports back to me of veterans having to undertake fewer medical tests as a result of that referral than they otherwise might have been asked to take by a treating doctor when these weren't required for claim decisions.

So I just want to frame it in a context, Senator Shoebridge, where the decisions the government has made about integrity and compliance reflect increasing trends in data and in behaviour that the department has moved quickly to respond to—that we work collaboratively and cooperatively with the vast majority of medical professionals, but we don't resile from taking action where there are observed behaviours and billing practices that are inappropriate for veterans and for the Australian taxpayer.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Where your data has identified that as a potential in relation to a medical practitioner, that may well be one thing. But I'll just read you a quote from an email that we got from a doctor: 'Longstanding GP clinics are being treated as though they're akin to the former Rosemary Centre. Despite operating lawfully and appropriately for many years, this approach effectively treats doctors as suspect or criminal without evidence simply because they provide care to veterans.'

I could read you a bunch of these. Doctors are saying to me—

Senator SCARR: And to me.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: and to Senator Scarr, that when you're actually treated like a criminal suspect because you're providing care to veterans it makes you not want to provide care to veterans. I fully support identifying fraud and I fully support systems that identify fraud and misbehaviour, but you need to get the balance right. What I'm hearing from doctors is that you're treating them like criminals because they're caring for veterans. And if you're not getting that feedback through your own channels then I don't think you're listening.

Ms Frame : I have not been receiving that feedback, that most medical professionals feel that way. There is a very small number from whom I have been receiving feedback that they are unhappy about actions taken by the department. That is to be anticipated when compliance action is being undertaken. But I have not been receiving feedback from many medical professionals or from our Chief Health Officer, who is a general practitioner and works extensively with general practitioners, that there is a widespread feeling of being persecuted or treated poorly by DVA.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: Could we go to this differential that's paid. Until the last few months, I wasn't aware that different doctors were being paid different rates to provide the same assessment, but that is what I understand happens on the ground—the exact same assessment, page numbers, condition type. Different doctors are being paid different amounts based on longstanding practice or other factors. Is that what's happening?

Mr Kefford : In relation to compensation reports, yes.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: The immediate concern that raises with me is that, if the department can choose to pay one group of doctors a higher rate for providing medical reports than it does for another group of doctors, the department would have an institutional interest in restraining spending, and therefore those doctors who write meaner and harder reports may well be given higher pay and encouraged to write more reports, while those doctors—treating doctors and others—who write supportive reports may well be paid lower rates because it's inconvenient when they write supporting reports. That's the immediate concern that comes to me, and I can tell you it's the concern that comes to veterans.

Ms Frame : That's not correct.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: You must have data on what rates are being paid to treating doctors for reports—as opposed to mlcoa, for example. You must have that data.

Ms Frame : I'm going to pass to Mr Kefford, but I would just like to open by saying the practice of paying what doctors bill—I'll just clarify that. We pay what the doctors say it cost them. It is the practice of DVA to pay that money to medical professionals. That has been longstanding practice since well before I was secretary. What we moved to do in recent weeks, as Mr Kefford explained, was in response to a concern about inequity in what was being sought, with some doctors billing amounts that simply didn't seem to be comparable to the work that was undertaken. It was nothing to do with what claims were there or what they were seeking for veterans, but it didn't seem to be comparable to the work that was undertaken. What we did was develop guidance for fees that we expect to be reasonable. We have moved to provide that schedule, which Mr Kefford said we will provide to the committee, in direct response to the issue you are raising.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: I have before acknowledged when the department has done good work. If you're stepping in to try to address this concern, maybe we can step through—if you're trying to address the concern of inequities. From my perspective, I've seen many statutory schemes in operation, and I've never seen them pay different rates to different providers for the exact same work. It just sends warning bells off, particularly in circumstances where there are a lot of veterans being directed to one provider, mlcoa. It just sets off warning bells to a highly sensitive community. Can you provide to us what the average fees provided for different reports are for mlcoa as against treating doctors. Are you able to provide that? I'm not expecting you to be able to do it now. Can you provide that on notice.

Ms Frame : We can definitely do it on notice. We can provide you more information now.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: If you could.

Ms Frame : I would also say that the foundational approach is that the veterans seek their own doctor. That continues to be the practice.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: And can you, on notice, provide over time whatever change is happening in the numbers of these assessment reports that are coming from treating doctors, which in my view is far and away preferable.

Ms Frame : I agree.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: They know the patient; they've got a relationship. The numbers, the proportion that are coming from treating doctors as opposed to external experts such as mlcoa—can you provide that going back, if you can, over five years so we can get a sense of what's happening, because some data here would be really helpful for the debate.

Ms Frame : We will get you some data.

Mr Kefford : The distinction I would draw, though—I'll ask Mr Brown, in a moment, to step through the basis on which we arrived at the newly updated recommended fees in the schedule that was released in February. What I would point out, though, is that the purpose of the mlcoa contract is different. What I could say about the data now is that there has been an increase in the last, say, 12 months as we have moved to refer more to independent examinations because we've had integrity concerns about the providers—again, not other than in relation to particular providers. I think the other point to make in this context is that where there are investigations, and there have been, there's a much more detailed follow-up with the provider concerned.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: The other data point that I think would be incredibly useful, for getting a handle on and maybe putting to bed concerns or highlighting concerns—I don't know what the data shows—is, to the extent you're able to assess it, whether mlcoa reports support or don't support claims as against treating doctors. Do you have any sense that they are—

Ms Frame : We might also include commercial advocates there.

Senator SHOEBRIDGE: If you can break it down into that as well. It may well be that commercial advocates have their own concerns. If we can have commercial advocates, mlcoa and treating doctors, we might get a sense of what's actually happening on the ground.

CHAIR: I'm just mindful we have very limited time. Mr Kefford, can you just answer, and then I'll have to move the call around.

Mr Kefford : I'll be brief. The only point I'll make in relation to the mlcoa contract is we have no say over what the doctors write. We pay for it to happen, so we pay for the report from the doctor, but we have no control over what they write.

CHAIR: I'll have to come back to you. Now I want to come to Senator Pocock and then Senator Scarr again.

Senator DAVID POCOCK: Thank you for your time. Sorry we didn't get to you during Senate estimates. Secretary, I have an email from a DVA delegate in the Client Benefits Division, which I'm happy to circulate and seek to table. It's very short, so I'll just read it out: 'Hi. I would like all clinical notes from April 2023 as the date you confirmed you started seeing him'—the veteran—'for any and all medical conditions, please.
